paragraphs.heading: Waves made by a spinning planet
paragraphs.text: Rossby waves, also called planetary waves, are a kind of wave that arises on its own in fluids that rotate. They appear in the air and the oceans of Earth and of other planets, because those planets spin. The Swedish-born American meteorologist Carl-Gustaf Arvid Rossby first identified them in Earth's atmosphere in 1939.

paragraphs.heading: How they work
paragraphs.text: On a spinning planet, moving air or water is turned rightward north of the equator and leftward south of it. Fluid heading from the equator toward the North Pole drifts east, and fluid heading back toward the equator drifts west. This turning effect, the Coriolis effect, grows stronger or weaker with latitude, and that change is what creates Rossby waves. On Earth the crest of a Rossby wave always moves partly westward. A whole group of these waves, though, can travel either way: short ones tend to drift east as a group and long ones west.

paragraphs.heading: Bends in the jet stream
paragraphs.text: In Earth's atmosphere, Rossby waves are huge meanders in the high-altitude winds, and they strongly shape the weather. They are easy to spot as the jet stream's large bends, usually four to six of them. When the bends grow very deep, pools of cold or warm air break off and become weak cyclones and anticyclones. These drive day-to-day weather in the mid-latitudes. Rossby waves also help explain why Eastern Canada and the Northeast United States are chillier than Western Europe at matching latitudes.

paragraphs.heading: Slow waves in the ocean
paragraphs.text: In the ocean, Rossby waves are large-scale waves found within an ocean basin. They travel along the thermocline, the border where the ocean's warm top layer meets its cold depths. They are very low: centimetres high at the surface and metres high at the thermocline, while atmospheric ones swing by hundreds of kilometres. They take their push from wind blowing across the surface, and they can need months to cross an ocean.

paragraphs.heading: Seen by satellites
paragraphs.text: Ocean Rossby waves raise and lower the sea surface, but they are so long that they were hard to detect until satellites began measuring sea height. Satellite records have since confirmed them and shown them moving steadily across every ocean basin, especially at low and middle latitudes. Their crossing times grow longer farther from the equator. In the Pacific, a wave near the equator may cross in months, while one nearer the poles may take decades.

paragraphs.heading: On other worlds
paragraphs.text: Like Kelvin waves, Rossby waves in the air can form on any rotating planet that has an atmosphere. The Y-shaped cloud pattern on Venus is put down to Kelvin and Rossby waves. Scientists have also suggested that Rossby waves cause the six-sided cloud pattern at Saturn's north pole.
